Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let gateway = PaymentGateway { endpoint: "https://gateway.internal".into(), }; Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { gateway }) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth failure goes to // "payments.dlq" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dlq") .include(on_dead_letter) }) } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let gateway = PaymentGateway { endpoint: "https://gateway.internal".into(), }; Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { gateway }) }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth failure goes to // "payments.dlq" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include( subscriber("payments", Charge) .map_source(|_| payments()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dlq") .include( subscriber("payments.dlq", OnDeadLetter) .map_source(|_| dead_letters()) .build(), ) }) } The dead-letter topic is read by an ordinary subscription: Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs /// The dead-letter consumer is an ordinary subscription. The framework's retry-count header says /// how many times the payment was delivered before it was carried here. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments.dlq").group("payments-dlq").start(StartOffset::Earliest))] async fn on_dead_letter(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs /// The dead-letter consumer is an ordinary subscription. The framework's retry-count header says /// how many times the payment was delivered before it was carried here. struct OnDeadLetter; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), AppState> for OnDeadLetter { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::error!(payment.id, deliveries, "payment dead-lettered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn dead_letters() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments.dlq") .group("payments-dlq") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) }

retry_after(delay) asks for a later delivery: the runtime republishes a copy to the subscription with its delivery count in a header. Kafka holds no record back and counts no deliveries, so the runtime does both. It settles the delivery, waits out the delay and publishes a copy of the record, payload and headers, to the topic the subscription reads. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER incremented, and the handler reads it like any other header. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at-most-once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. max_attempts(n) caps the deliveries of one record at the mount site, the first one included. Under a cap every retry, an immediate one too, travels as such a copy, because the count lives in the header. The delivery that reaches the cap goes to the dead-letter topic. The copies leave through the Retry slot, which out_retry replaces. A subscription over several topics names where its copies go, as ToSourceTopic shows.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_retries.rs /// A transient failure asks for a later delivery. Kafka cannot hold a record back, so the /// runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy to the topic this subscription reads, with /// the retry-count header incremented. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payments").group("payments-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, State(gateway): State<PaymentGateway>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { // Malformed input is not worth retrying: dropping it settles the offset. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } match gateway.charge(payment).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } } } examples/manual/kafka_retries.rs /// A transient failure asks for a later delivery. Kafka cannot hold a record back, so the /// runtime waits out the delay and publishes a copy to the topic this subscription reads, with /// the retry-count header incremented. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), AppState> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { // Malformed input is not worth retrying: dropping it settles the offset. return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.charge(payment).await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK)); } Ok(()) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

ToSourceTopic sends each retry copy back to the topic its delivery arrived on, for subscriptions over several topics. A KafkaTopic subscription reads one topic, and its retry copies go there. A KafkaTopics list or pattern and a KafkaPartitions reader have no single topic, so the mount site names one. ToSourceTopic is a transform of the Retry slot: .out_retry(Publish::default()).transform(ToSourceTopic). It reads each delivery's topic from its Kafka context, so a copy of an orders-us record goes back to orders-us. The context reaches the slot when the handler reads it: a Ctx<Topic> parameter, or a manual body typed over KafkaContext. A batch handler carries no per-record topic, so a batch registration names a fixed topic instead. .out_retry(Publish::default()).to(topic) sends every copy to that one topic; a pattern that matches it reads the copies back. A registration over several topics that names neither does not start.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// One subscription reads both regions. Reading the topic is also what hands the Kafka context /// to the retry position, where `ToSourceTopic` reads it. #[subscriber(KafkaTopics::new(["orders-eu", "orders-us"]).group("orders-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn reserve( order: &Order, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>, State(warehouse): State<Arc<Warehouse>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = warehouse.reserve(order) { tracing::warn!(order.id, %topic, err, "warehouse unavailable, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// One subscription reads both regions. A body typed over `KafkaContext` hands that context to /// the retry position, where `ToSourceTopic` reads it. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Order, (), (), KafkaContext, AppState> for Reserve { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext, AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let topic = ctx.context(Topic); if let Err(err) = ctx.state().warehouse.reserve(order) { tracing::warn!(order.id, %topic, err, "warehouse unavailable, retrying"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "stock reserved"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn regions() -> KafkaTopics { KafkaTopics::new(["orders-eu", "orders-us"]) .group("orders-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) } Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A copy goes back to the topic its delivery arrived on. b.include(reserve) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.orders") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) // Every copy goes to one topic. `.to(topic)` belongs to the publisher the copies // leave through, so it follows `out_retry`. .include(post_entry) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.ledger") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("ledger.retry") }) } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = AppState> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A copy goes back to the topic its delivery arrived on. b.include( subscriber("orders-eu,orders-us", Reserve) .map_source(|_| regions()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.orders") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) // Every copy goes to one topic. `.to(topic)` belongs to the publisher the copies // leave through, so it follows `out_retry`. .include( subscriber("^ledger\\..*", PostEntry) .map_source(|_| ledgers()) .build(), ) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("dlq.ledger") .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("ledger.retry") }) }

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// A pattern reads every ledger topic there is; its copies go to one retry topic the pattern /// also matches, so they come back to this subscription. #[subscriber(KafkaTopicPattern::new("^ledger\\..*").group("ledger-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn post_entry(entry: &Entry, State(ledger): State<Arc<Ledger>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = ledger.post(entry) { tracing::warn!(entry.order_id, err, "ledger unavailable, retrying"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_source_topic.rs /// A pattern reads every ledger topic there is; its copies go to one retry topic the pattern /// also matches, so they come back to this subscription. struct PostEntry; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), (), AppState> for PostEntry { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if let Err(err) = ctx.state().ledger.post(entry) { tracing::warn!(entry.order_id, err, "ledger unavailable, retrying"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } ready(Ok(())) } } fn ledgers() -> KafkaTopicPattern { KafkaTopics::pattern("^ledger\\..*") .group("ledger-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

Commit::Tracked commits below the lowest unsettled delivery, so a retry comes back and nothing is committed past it. The subscription stores a position only when a handler settles a delivery. The stored position is the offset just below the lowest delivery still in flight, so handlers that finish out of order, on several workers, never commit past an unfinished one. librdkafka's timer commits the stored position in the background and once more when the consumer closes. An ack and a drop settle the offset. A retry hands the delivery back to its subscription, which delivers it again before the records behind it. Until it is settled, the group's committed position stays below it, so a crash or a rebalance brings it to the next member. Offsets the consumer never receives, such as transaction markers and compacted records, do not hold the position back. Tracked with an idempotent producer gives at-least-once from input to output, as Durability shows.

Macros Manual examples/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// A charge the gateway turned away comes back on this subscription before anything behind it, /// and the group commits nothing past it until it is settled. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("charges").group("payments").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn take_charge(charge: &Charge, State(gateway): State<Arc<Gateway>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if let Err(err) = gateway.charge(charge) { tracing::warn!(%err, "charge retried"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(charge.id, "charge taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_settlement_commit.rs /// A charge the gateway turned away comes back on this subscription before anything behind it, /// and the group commits nothing past it until it is settled. struct TakeCharge; impl Handle<Charge, (), (), (), AppState> for TakeCharge { fn handle( &self, charge: &Charge, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.charge(charge) { tracing::warn!(%err, "charge retried"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(charge.id, "charge taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn payments() -> KafkaTopic { KafkaTopic::new("charges") .group("payments") .commit(Commit::Tracked) }

A topic name in #[subscriber] reads that topic in the broker's default group; a descriptor carries every other setting. #[subscriber("orders")] reads the topic orders. Kafka reads a topic only through a consumer group, and a bare name names none, so the group comes from KafkaBroker::default_group. A subscription with no group, on a broker with no default group, stops the service at startup with an error that names the subscription. Two subscriptions of one name and one group are two members of that group: each record goes to one of them. Every other setting of a subscription belongs to a descriptor: KafkaTopic for one topic, KafkaTopics for several topics, KafkaTopicPattern for every topic a regex matches, and KafkaPartitions for named partitions. A descriptor goes where the name goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the name to subscriber(name, body), and a descriptor joins the chain through map_source. A subscription is open once its group has assigned it its partitions, so everything published after startup reaches it. Startup waits for that assignment up to KafkaBroker::assignment_timeout, 60 seconds by default.

The topic orders, read in the group orders-svc. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the group comes from the broker. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place)) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the topic `orders`; the group comes from the broker. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders-svc"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build())) }

Assignment picks the consumer group's rebalance strategy, eager or cooperative sticky. A group hands each partition of its topics to one member, and hands them out again when a member joins or leaves. The setting is librdkafka's partition.assignment.strategy, written on the descriptor with assignment. Assignment::Range and Assignment::RoundRobin are eager: every member gives up all its partitions at each rebalance, and the group stops reading until the new assignment lands. Assignment::CooperativeSticky is incremental: only the partitions that change hands move, and the rest keep flowing during the rebalance. Without the setting librdkafka uses range,roundrobin. Every member of one group must use the same family: librdkafka refuses a cooperative member in an eager group, and the error surfaces on the subscription. KafkaPartitions joins no group and has no assignment.

A cooperative sticky group reads every shipment once, whichever member holds its partition. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_assignment.rs /// Ships each shipment; a rebalance moves only the partitions that change hands. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("warehouse.shipments") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) )] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_assignment.rs /// Ships each shipment it reads. struct Ship; impl Handle<Shipment> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.id, "shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(servers: &str, group: &str) -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("warehouse", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A rebalance moves only the partitions that change hands. let shipments = KafkaTopic::new("warehouse.shipments") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky); b.include( subscriber("warehouse.shipments", Ship) .build() .map_source(|_| shipments), ) }) }

A slice handler reads one fetched delivery plus what librdkafka already holds, up to the size the mount site names. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The size travels down to the consumer's poll, which never hands the body more than n records. librdkafka fetches records ahead in the background, and a batch takes what it already holds without waiting for more. So a batch is often smaller than n, and a quiet topic yields batches of one. The runtime lends the subscription one slot that every batch fills, so a batch allocates nothing. One outcome settles every record of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles record i with outcome i. Under Commit::Tracked a record that asks to come back holds the committed position in front of it until it settles; a process that stops first replays the acked records behind it too. A retry_after in a batch becomes a copy published back to the topic after the delay, so the registration names its retry publisher with .out_retry(policy). How much librdkafka queues locally is a consumer property, set through the descriptor's passthrough (queued.max.messages.kbytes, fetch.queue.backoff.ms). workers(n) keeps up to n batches in flight at once. A batch body reads a KafkaBatchContext, which carries the seek handle and no per-record field. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles record by record.

Three orders waiting in the consumer's queue arrive in one call. Macros Manual examples/kafka_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip; one outcome settles the whole batch. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("orders-svc").commit(Commit::Tracked), workers(4) )] async fn store(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(store.batch(nonzero!(64))) }) } examples/manual/kafka_batches.rs /// Stores a batch of orders in one round-trip; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct Store; impl Handle<[Order]> for Store { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked); // At most 64 orders per call, up to four calls at once. b.include( subscriber("orders", Store) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .workers(nonzero!(4)) .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ) }) }

Only the unsettled payment comes back, as a copy published after the delay. Macros Manual examples/kafka_batches.rs /// One outcome per payment, in slice order: only the unsettled ones come back. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("queued.max.messages.kbytes", "1024") )] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.settled { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A delayed retry is a copy published back to the topic after the delay. b.include(reconcile.batch(nonzero!(16))) .out_retry(Publish::default()) }) } examples/manual/kafka_batches.rs /// One outcome per payment, in slice order: only the unsettled ones come back. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.settled { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let payments = KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("queued.max.messages.kbytes", "1024"); // A delayed retry is a copy published back to the topic after the delay. b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build() .map_source(|_| payments), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) }) }

KafkaPartitions reads exactly the partitions it names, joins no group and never rebalances. KafkaPartitions::new takes the topic and its partition numbers. It suits a reader pinned to a partition, an inspection or replay tool, and one consumer per partition. The reader takes no part in the group protocol, so group members on the same topic neither see it nor take its partitions away. A group stays optional and decides only where offsets go. With group the reader commits into that group without joining it. Without a group it commits nothing, so start must name Earliest or Latest: Committed has nothing to resume from and stops the service at startup. commit, lane_key and config work as on KafkaTopic; Commit::Transactional stops the service at startup, because an exactly-once pipeline commits through the group protocol. Under the default lane key each named partition gets a lane of its own. The subscription's name is the topic. No publish addresses a subset of partitions, so a registration names where a retry copy goes, as the example does with .out_retry(policy).to("orders.retry").

Partition 0 of orders, read from its first record by a service that names no group. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_partitions.rs /// Inspects partition 0 of `orders` from its first record, with no group of its own. #[subscriber(KafkaPartitions::new("orders", [0]).start(StartOffset::Earliest))] async fn inspect(order: &Order, Ctx(offset): Ctx<Offset>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, offset, "partition 0"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { // The broker names no group, and the reader needs none. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inspector", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No publish reaches exactly these partitions, so a retried order goes to a topic of // its own. b.include(inspect) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("orders.retry") }) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_partitions.rs /// Logs each order with its offset in the partition. struct Inspect; impl Handle<Order, (), (), KafkaContext> for Inspect { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, offset = ctx.context(Offset), "partition 0"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // The broker names no group, and the reader needs none. let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inspector", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Partition 0 of `orders`, from its first record. let partition = KafkaPartitions::new("orders", [0]).start(StartOffset::Earliest); // No publish reaches exactly these partitions, so a retried order goes to a topic of // its own. b.include( subscriber("orders", Inspect) .build() .map_source(|_| partition), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("orders.retry") }) }

KafkaTopic reads one topic in one consumer group, with its start offset, commit mode, assignment and lane key. KafkaTopic::new takes the topic, and every other setting is optional. An unset setting keeps librdkafka's own default; the crate adds none of its own. group names the consumer group and overrides the broker's default_group. start is the start offset of a group that has committed nothing yet. commit is the commit mode, which decides what an ack does. assignment is the group's rebalance strategy, and lane_key is what keyed lanes are keyed by. config passes any other consumer property to librdkafka. The subscription's name is the topic: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A publish to the topic reaches every group that reads it, so a delayed retry copy goes back to the topic with no setting at the mount site. A topic name that Kafka refuses, or a name that starts with ^, stops the service at startup; a pattern is KafkaTopicPattern. schema turns on schema checking for the topic.

Every order of orders is confirmed by the group orders-workers, and the confirmation goes to the topic its type declares. Macros Manual examples/kafka_topics.rs /// Confirms every order of the topic `orders`, as a member of the group `orders-workers`. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .commit(Commit::Tracked) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) .config("fetch.min.bytes", "1024"), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: true, } } examples/manual/kafka_topics.rs /// Confirms every order it reads. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: true, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The topic `orders`, read as a member of the group `orders-workers`. let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .start(StartOffset::Earliest) .commit(Commit::Tracked) .assignment(Assignment::CooperativeSticky) .config("fetch.min.bytes", "1024"); b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ) }) }

KafkaTopics reads a list of topics through one consumer and one group, and each delivery names its topic. KafkaTopics::new takes the topics, and and_topic adds one more. The group settings are the ones KafkaTopic has: group, start, commit, assignment, lane_key and config. Every topic of the list shares the handler, so every topic carries the handler's payload type. Ctx<Topic> binds the topic a delivery came from. The subscription's name is the list joined with commas, orders,cancellations here. No one publish reaches a list again, so a registration over it names where a retry copy goes: .out_retry(policy).to(topic), or ToSourceTopic to send each copy back to the topic it came from. A registration that names neither stops the service at startup. schema(topic, namespace) turns on schema checking for one topic of the list, addressed by its name. Every topic a regex matches is a pattern, a descriptor of its own.

Order events from two topics become one history, and each entry names the topic of its event. Macros Manual examples/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Reads two topics through one consumer of the group `order-history`. #[subscriber( KafkaTopics::new(["orders", "cancellations"]).group("order-history"), reply )] async fn record(event: &OrderEvent, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HistoryEntry { HistoryEntry { id: event.id, topic: topic.to_string(), } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // No one topic reaches a topic set again, so the mount site says where a retried // event goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include(record) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) }) } examples/manual/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Answers each event with a history entry naming the topic it came from. struct Record; impl Handle<OrderEvent, HistoryEntry, (), KafkaContext> for Record { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<HistoryEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(HistoryEntry { id: event.id, topic: ctx.context(Topic).to_string(), })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Two topics through one consumer of the group `order-history`. let events = KafkaTopics::new(["orders", "cancellations"]).group("order-history"); // No one topic reaches a topic set again, so the mount site says where a retried // event goes: back to the topic it came from. b.include( subscriber("orders,cancellations", Record) .reply() .build() .map_source(|_| events), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) }) }

LaneKey decides what workers(n, by_key) keys a lane by: the source partition, or the record key. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes: deliveries with one lane key run in order on one lane, and different keys run at once. On Kafka the descriptor's lane_key decides what that key is. LaneKey::Partition, the default, keys a lane by the partition the record came from, Kafka's own unit of order. Everything one partition delivers then runs in order, keyless records included, and partitions run side by side. LaneKey::RecordKey keys a lane by the record's native key, which is finer than a partition. One key's records stay in order, and records of different keys run at once even inside one partition. A keyless record has no lane key under RecordKey; it rotates over the lanes and loses its partition order. The publish side sets the record key from the partition-key header, so a record published with a key reaches its lane by that key. The manual form writes the lanes as .workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

Two tenants' orders, each order a second of work: lanes by record key run the tenants side by side, two seconds in all. Macros Manual examples/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by record key: one tenant's orders run in order, different tenants at once, /// even inside one partition. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("orders").group("orders-workers").lane_key(LaneKey::RecordKey), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn on_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { process(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by record key: one tenant's orders run in order, different tenants at once, /// even inside one partition. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders") .group("orders-workers") .lane_key(LaneKey::RecordKey); b.include( subscriber("orders", Process) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build() .map_source(|_| orders), ) }) }

The same four orders on a topic with one partition take four seconds: the partition is one lane. Macros Manual examples/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by source partition, the default: everything one partition delivers runs in /// order on one lane, keyless records included. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("audit").group("audit-workers"), workers(8, by_key))] async fn on_audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { process(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_keys.rs /// Eight lanes by source partition, the default: everything one partition delivers runs in /// order on one lane, keyless records included. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let audit = KafkaTopic::new("audit").group("audit-workers"); b.include( subscriber("audit", Process) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build() .map_source(|_| audit), ) }) }

A descriptor's config passes any consumer property; one the commit mode owns is refused at startup, naming the property. KafkaTopic::config, and the same method on KafkaTopics and KafkaPartitions, sets one librdkafka consumer property by its name. It reaches the properties the descriptor has no typed option for: fetch sizes, queue limits, timeouts. The passthrough applies last, so it wins over the typed options and over the broker-wide configuration. A property the commit mode owns is the exception. Under Commit::Tracked and Commit::Transactional the crate computes the committed position itself, through enable.auto.offset.store and enable.auto.commit. A passthrough that sets either one would leave the position to librdkafka while every ack decided nothing. So the subscription refuses to open, and the startup error names the subscription and the property. Commit::Auto owns neither property and takes both from the passthrough. A property for every consumer of the broker goes on KafkaBroker instead.

fetch.queue.backoff.ms shortens the pause librdkafka takes when a partition's local queue is full, from a second to 10 ms. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_passthrough.rs /// Settles payments; librdkafka pauses a full partition for 10 ms instead of a second. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10") )] async fn settle(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.id, "settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_passthrough.rs /// Settles every payment it reads. struct Settle; impl Handle<Payment> for Settle { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.id, "settled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // librdkafka pauses a full partition for 10 ms instead of a second. let payments = KafkaTopic::new("payments") .group("payments-svc") .commit(Commit::Tracked) .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10"); b.include( subscriber("payments", Settle) .build() .map_source(|_| payments), ) }) }

KafkaTopicPattern reads every topic a librdkafka regex starting with ^ matches, those created later included. The leading ^ is how librdkafka tells a pattern from a topic name. A pattern without it stops the service at startup, because librdkafka would subscribe to it as a literal name. KafkaTopicPattern::new takes the pattern, and and_pattern adds another one to the same subscription. KafkaTopics::pattern builds the same descriptor; the #[subscriber] attribute takes the type its constructor names, so the attribute starts from KafkaTopicPattern::new. The group settings are the ones KafkaTopic has. The consumer finds a topic created after startup on its next metadata refresh, and the group then assigns its partitions. A new topic is read from where the start offset puts it. The subscription's name is the pattern itself. A delivery names the topic it came from through Ctx<Topic>, and a retry copy needs a destination named at the mount site, as on KafkaTopics. Sets of the matched topics opt into schema checking with .schema(pattern, namespace).

Every topic under audit. is archived; auditing is not. Macros Manual examples/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Reads every topic whose name starts with `audit.`, those created later included. #[subscriber(KafkaTopicPattern::new("^audit\\..*").group("audit-archive"))] async fn archive(event: &OrderEvent, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.id, %topic, "archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A retried event goes back to the topic it came from. b.include(archive) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) }) } examples/manual/kafka_multi_topic.rs /// Archives an event, logging the topic it came from. struct Archive; impl Handle<OrderEvent, (), (), KafkaContext> for Archive { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.id, topic = %ctx.context(Topic), "archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Every topic whose name starts with `audit.`, those created later included. let audit = KafkaTopics::pattern("^audit\\..*").group("audit-archive"); // A retried event goes back to the topic it came from. b.include( subscriber("^audit\\..*", Archive) .build() .map_source(|_| audit), ) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .transform(ToSourceTopic) }) }

schema(namespace) on a descriptor checks at startup that the topic's registry subjects exist and declare records of that namespace. A topic opts in one by one; a topic without schema is checked against no registry and costs nothing. The namespace is the one its records carry: com.acme.orders for com.acme.orders.Order. The subjects follow TopicNameStrategy: orders-value for the payload of orders, orders-key for its key. Schema::namespace names other subjects with .value(..) and .key(..); a plain string is the namespace with the default subjects. The check reads the registry of KafkaBroker::schema_prefetch, once per topic, while the subscription opens. A broker with no registry stops the service at startup when a topic opts in. What stops the service, with the topic, the subject, where its name came from, and the fix in the error: the value subject is missing from the registry; the newest schema of the value subject declares no record of the namespace; a key subject named with .key(..) is missing; a key subject that exists declares records, none of them of the namespace. A key subject the topic's name gives may be missing: a topic with plain string keys registers none. An Avro subject declares its record, or each record of a union; a Protobuf subject declares its top-level messages in its package. A JSON Schema names no record, so a JSON subject is checked for presence only. Each form opts in with the arguments it needs: KafkaTopic::schema(namespace) for its one topic; KafkaTopics::schema(topic, namespace) for one topic of the list, addressed by name; a name the list does not hold stops the service and names the list; KafkaTopicPattern::schema(pattern, namespace) for a set of the matched topics. The sets of a pattern narrow in the order they are written: a topic takes the first set whose pattern it matches. Each topic of a set has its own default subjects (orders.eu-value), and an override names one subject for the whole set. A matched topic that no set takes is not checked. The topics the cluster holds when the subscription opens are checked at startup. A topic created later is checked when the group first assigns it to the member, and a mismatch then is logged.

orders is checked against orders-value; of the two listed topics, returns names its own value subject. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_schema.rs /// `orders` is checked against `orders-value`, the subject its name gives. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("orders").schema("com.acme.orders"))] async fn on_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Each listed topic opts in by name; `returns` names its value subject. #[subscriber( KafkaTopics::new(["refunds", "returns"]) .schema("refunds", "com.acme.orders") .schema("returns", Schema::namespace("com.acme.orders").value("returns-v2")) )] async fn on_settlement(order: &Order, Ctx(topic): Ctx<Topic>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, %topic, "settled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(registry: &str) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(SchemaRegistry::new(registry)); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_prefetch(prefetch); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(on_order) .include(on_settlement) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("settlements.retry") }) } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_schema.rs /// Places an order. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(registry: &str) -> impl App { let prefetch = SchemaPrefetch::new(SchemaRegistry::new(registry)); let broker = KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]) .default_group("orders-svc") .schema_prefetch(prefetch); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = KafkaTopic::new("orders").schema("com.acme.orders"); let settlements = KafkaTopics::new(["refunds", "returns"]) .schema("refunds", "com.acme.orders") .schema( "returns", Schema::namespace("com.acme.orders").value("returns-v2"), ); // `orders` is checked against `orders-value`, the subject its name gives. b.include(subscriber(orders, Place).build()) // Each listed topic opts in by name; `returns` names its value subject. .include(subscriber(settlements, Place).build()) .out_retry(Publish::default()) .to("settlements.retry") }) }

StartOffset says where a group starts on a partition with no committed offset: committed reset, earliest or latest. A group resumes from its committed offset whenever it has a valid one. StartOffset applies only where it has none: before the group's first commit on a partition, and after retention deleted the record a committed offset pointed at. The setting is librdkafka's auto.offset.reset, written on the descriptor with start. StartOffset::Committed, the default, leaves the choice to librdkafka, which resets to the end of the log. StartOffset::Earliest starts at the oldest record the topic retains. StartOffset::Latest starts at the end of the log: only records published after the subscription opened arrive. The second case matters for a group that sat idle longer than the topic's retention: with the default it skips to the end instead of reading what is left. A position that applies on every startup, whatever the group committed, is start_at.

A new archive group reads the invoices the topic held before the group existed. Macros Manual examples/kafka_subscriptions_start_offset.rs /// Archives every invoice: a new archive group starts at the oldest record the topic retains. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("ledger.invoices").start(StartOffset::Earliest))] async fn archive(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "archived"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_subscriptions_start_offset.rs /// Archives every invoice it reads. struct Archive; impl Handle<Invoice> for Archive { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "archived"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(servers: &str, group: &str) -> impl App { let broker = KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group(group); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // A new archive group starts at the oldest record the topic retains. let invoices = KafkaTopic::new("ledger.invoices").start(StartOffset::Earliest); b.include( subscriber("ledger.invoices", Archive) .build() .map_source(|_| invoices), ) }) }

TestApp::start connects KafkaBroker to an in-process cluster with topics, groups, offsets and transactions. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The cluster has no settings of its own. It reads what librdkafka would read: the broker's config and producer_config, each descriptor's options, and librdkafka's defaults for the rest. A property name or value librdkafka refuses fails TestApp::start as it fails the connect. The cluster keeps Kafka's semantics. A topic comes into being with one partition when a record is produced to it or a subscription names it. Each consumer group reads a record once, and every group reads its own copy. The subscription's commit mode decides what is committed, and a seek moves the partitions the subscription reads. A read_committed reader, librdkafka's default, sees a transaction's records when it commits and never after an abort. The cluster refuses what a cluster refuses: a partition the topic lacks, an illegal topic name, a record over message.max.bytes. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply or a committed transaction included. The assertions that follow read finished state. What only a cluster has, such as a topic with several partitions or the timing of a real group join, is for a live test.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-rdkafka = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes a payment and reads how the handler settled it. Macros Manual examples/kafka_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_is_accepted() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/kafka_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_is_accepted() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } A refund publishes its lines inside one transaction, and the handler commits or aborts it. The topic shows the lines of the committed refund and none of the aborted one. Macros Manual examples/kafka_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_aborted_refund_publishes_no_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let refund = Refund { order_id: 1, lines: 3, settle: false, }; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&refund) .publish() .await?; // A `read_committed` reader, librdkafka's default, never sees an aborted transaction. tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<RefundLine>("refund-lines") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn a_committed_refund_publishes_every_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let refund = Refund { order_id: 2, lines: 3, settle: true, }; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&refund) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<RefundLine>("refund-lines") .assert_called(3); Ok(()) } examples/manual/kafka_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_aborted_refund_publishes_no_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let refund = Refund { order_id: 1, lines: 3, settle: false, }; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&refund) .publish() .await?; // A `read_committed` reader, librdkafka's default, never sees an aborted transaction. tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<RefundLine>("refund-lines") .assert_not_called(); Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn a_committed_refund_publishes_every_line() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let refund = Refund { order_id: 2, lines: 3, settle: true, }; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&refund) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .published::<RefundLine>("refund-lines") .assert_called(3); Ok(()) }

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running Kafka, for what only a cluster has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so startup probes the cluster and every group joins it for real. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. A consumer group takes a few seconds to form on a cluster, so a Kafka test gives it thirty. The live mode is for what the in-process cluster leaves out: a topic created with several partitions, the cooperative assignment that keeps partitions sticky, retention, and the timing of a group join. A cluster keeps what earlier runs left in it. Each run reads in a consumer group of its own, and creates its topics before the app starts: a group assigned a topic created after it subscribed reads from the end of the log, past the record that created the topic. In the example, live::url returns the cluster's address from KAFKA_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no cluster. A job that stood a cluster up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, which just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the cluster at KAFKA_TEST_URL. Macros Manual examples/kafka_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn accepts_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("testing-live-payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start(app("kafka:9092", "payments-svc")).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_stand() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(servers) = live::url("KAFKA_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; ensure_topic(&servers, "testing-live-payments").await?; // A group of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run committed is read. let group = format!("payments-{}", process::id()); // A group forms on a cluster in seconds, more than the default ten-second bound allows for. let tb = TestApp::start_live_within(app(&servers, &group), Duration::from_secs(30)).await?; accepts_a_payment(tb).await } examples/manual/kafka_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn accepts_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>() .subscriber("testing-live-payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start(app("kafka:9092", "payments-svc")).await?).await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_stand() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(servers) = live::url("KAFKA_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; ensure_topic(&servers, "testing-live-payments").await?; // A group of this run's own, so nothing an earlier run committed is read. let group = format!("payments-{}", process::id()); // A group forms on a cluster in seconds, more than the default ten-second bound allows for. let tb = TestApp::start_live_within(app(&servers, &group), Duration::from_secs(30)).await?; accepts_a_payment(tb).await }

transactional_id makes the publish policy transactional: publishes between begin and commit become visible together, or not at all. The policy it returns is KafkaTransactionalPublish, named TransactionalPublish in the prelude. It pairs into a KafkaTransactionalPublisher, which carries the core's TransactionalPublisher capability. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Marker> and calls begin_transaction, then commit or abort. The producer is created and its transactions initialized at startup, when the policy pairs, so the handler holds a fenced producer from its first delivery. Readers at Kafka's default read_committed isolation see the records of a transaction at its commit; an abort discards them on the broker. Outside an open transaction the publisher sends like a plain one. The transactional id is the fencing unit: initializing a producer with an id fences the previous producer that held it. So the id is stable and unique per running instance, for example one per replica. transaction_timeout bounds how long begin, commit and abort may block (30 seconds by default). It is the call deadline; Kafka's own transaction.timeout.ms is a producer property, set through producer_config. queue_timeout bounds the wait for space in librdkafka's local queue. One producer runs one transaction at a time. A second begin_transaction while one is open returns KafkaError::TransactionBusy, and a commit or abort with nothing open returns KafkaError::NoTransaction. So the handlers of a workers(n) pool do not share one transactional publisher; per_partition gives each source partition a publisher of its own. The test harness records what the handler sent through the slot, committed or not, while the topic shows only what was committed.

An order ships one record per item, in one transaction. An item without a name aborts the transaction, which discards the shipments already sent. Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; /// One shipment per item, published in one transaction. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { if shipments.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { // The shipments already sent belong to the transaction, so the abort discards them. if shipments.abort().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::warn!( order = order.id, "an item has no name, the order ships nothing" ); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { shipments.abort().await.ok(); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if shipments.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_transactions.rs struct Shipments; impl OutSlot for Shipments { const NAME: &'static str = "Shipments"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Shipments> for Shipment {} /// One shipment per item, published in one transaction. struct Ship; impl<S> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(S,)>> for Ship where S: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(S,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipments = outs.get(Shipments); if shipments.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { // The shipments already sent belong to the transaction, so the abort discards // them. if shipments.abort().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::warn!( order = order.id, "an item has no name, the order ships nothing" ); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if shipments.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { shipments.abort().await.ok(); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } if shipments.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { let shipments = Publish::default() .transactional_id("shipments-svc-1") .transaction_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("shipments-svc"), |b| b.include(ship).out(Shipments, shipments).build(), ) } examples/manual/kafka_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { let shipments = Publish::default() .transactional_id("shipments-svc-1") .transaction_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("shipments-svc"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()) .out(Shipments, shipments) .build() }, ) }

KafkaEosPublish commits consumed offsets inside the producer's transaction, so positions move atomically with the records published. It is the consume-transform-produce shape of Kafka (KIP-447), named EosPublish in the prelude. KafkaEosPublish::new takes the pipeline id, which is also the producer's transactional id. Each source subscription names the same id in Commit::Transactional: its consumer stops committing on its own, and the pipeline commits its offsets. One pipeline serves every lane of a workers(n, by_key) pool: publishes join the open transaction concurrently, and only the commit is exclusive. The pipeline works in windows. Every commit_interval (100 ms by default) it waits until the window's deliveries have settled, adds their positions and the group's metadata to the transaction, and commits. A record becomes visible at that commit, so end-to-end latency is at least the interval. A failed publish, a failed commit or a participant that does not settle in time aborts the window. The consumers then seek back to the last committed offsets, and the whole window is delivered and published again in a fresh transaction, so the output topic never holds a duplicate. A retry() from a participant holds its window until the transaction deadline, transaction_timeout. The retry_after copy does not apply to the pipeline's replies: a delayed copy would separate the record from its offset. The window's commit runs on the runtime the broker connected on, so a handler on a dedicated thread may open a window. The transactional commit needs consumer group membership. So Commit::Transactional is a KafkaTopic or KafkaTopics mode; KafkaPartitions, which joins no group, works with Commit::Auto and Commit::Tracked. A replying handler reaches the window through EosReplies, and a handler that publishes by hand through EosPipeline.

An order is priced, and the priced order commits together with the offset of the order it answers. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos.rs /// Prices an order; the subscription commits its offsets through the `pricing-1` pipeline. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("raw-orders").commit(Commit::Transactional("pricing-1".into())), reply )] async fn price(order: &Order) -> PricedOrder { PricedOrder { id: order.id, cents: order.cents, tax_cents: order.cents / 5, } } examples/manual/kafka_eos.rs /// Prices an order; the subscription commits its offsets through the `pricing-1` pipeline. struct Price; impl Handle<Order, PricedOrder> for Price { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<PricedOrder, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(PricedOrder { id: order.id, cents: order.cents, tax_cents: order.cents / 5, })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The policy's id is the pipeline the subscription names, and the producer's transactional id. let pipeline = EosPublish::new("pricing-1").commit_interval(Duration::from_millis(100)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("pricing-svc"), |b| b.include(price).out_reply(pipeline).transform(EosReplies), ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos.rs fn app() -> impl App { // The policy's id is the pipeline the subscription names, and the producer's transactional id. let pipeline = EosPublish::new("pricing-1").commit_interval(Duration::from_millis(100)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("pricing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("pricing-svc"), |b| { let orders = subscriber("raw-orders", Price) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("raw-orders").commit(Commit::Transactional("pricing-1".into())) }) .reply(); b.include(orders.build()) .out_reply(pipeline) .transform(EosReplies) }, ) }

EosWindow::publish_paired sends a record into the open window by hand, with the source coordinates the Source key gives. EosPipeline is the live form of EosPublish, so a slot bound to that policy holds one. A handler writes into the window through the slot's EosWindow capability, Out<impl EosWindow>, and the manual form names the slot's wired value. The delivery's coordinates are a SourceOffset, read with Ctx<Source> (context::keys::Source). window.publish_paired(&source, record, None) adds the record to the window and pairs it with that offset; the last argument is the per-call options, and None keeps the producer's own partition choice. A handler publishes as many records as it needs, then acks: the settled delivery is what lets the window commit. A failed publish poisons the window, which aborts and is delivered again, so the handler answers it with retry(). The record is an OutgoingMessage the handler encodes itself. A refused record comes back inside the error, so the handler still holds it. id returns the pipeline id.

A cart is split into one record per item, and every record commits with the cart's offset. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs /// Splits a cart into one record per item, all committed with the cart's offset. #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("carts").commit(Commit::Transactional("checkout-1".into())))] async fn split( cart: &Cart, Ctx(source): Ctx<Source>, Out(window): Out<impl EosWindow>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { for item in &cart.items { let line = CartLine { cart_id: cart.id, item: item.clone(), }; let Ok(payload) = serde_json::to_vec(&line) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let record = OutgoingMessage::new("cart-lines", payload.as_slice()); // A failed publish aborts the window, which redelivers the cart. if window.publish_paired(&source, record, None).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs /// Splits a cart into one record per item, all committed with the cart's offset. struct Split; impl<W> Handle<Cart, (), Outs<(W,)>, KafkaContext> for Split where W: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire = EosPipeline>, { async fn handle( &self, cart: &Cart, outs: &Outs<(W,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline: &EosPipeline = outs.get(DefaultSlot); let source = ctx.context(Source); for item in &cart.items { let line = CartLine { cart_id: cart.id, item: item.clone(), }; let Ok(payload) = serde_json::to_vec(&line) else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let record = OutgoingMessage::new("cart-lines", payload.as_slice()); // A failed publish aborts the window, which redelivers the cart. if pipeline.publish(&source, record, None).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("checkout-svc"), |b| { b.include(split) .out(DefaultSlot, EosPublish::new("checkout-1")) .build() }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_pipeline.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("checkout-svc"), |b| { let carts = subscriber("carts", Split).map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("carts").commit(Commit::Transactional("checkout-1".into())) }); b.include(carts.build()) .out(DefaultSlot, EosPublish::new("checkout-1")) .build() }, ) }

EosReplies joins every reply to the pipeline's open window, paired with its delivery's consumed offset. It is a publish transform for the reply position, written after the policy: .out_reply(EosPublish::new(id)).transform(EosReplies). A Commit::Transactional subscription marks each delivery with its source coordinates, and the transform carries them onto the reply. The pipeline reads them, pairs the reply with that offset, and drops them before the record is produced, so they never reach the topic. The handler only returns its value: it names no publisher and no offset. Without the transform, a reply carries no coordinates and its publish fails with KafkaError::InvalidOptions, so nothing leaves outside the window. A reply from a subscription in another commit mode fails the same way. A handler that settles without a reply, a drop or an Err(outcome), publishes nothing, and its offset still commits with the window.

A payment is booked on a pool of four lanes; a payment of zero is dropped. Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_replies.rs /// Books a payment; an empty one is dropped, and its offset still commits with the window. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("payments").commit(Commit::Transactional("ledger-1".into())), reply, workers(4, by_key) )] async fn book(payment: &Payment) -> Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome> { if payment.cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(LedgerEntry { payment_id: payment.id, cents: payment.cents, }) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_replies.rs /// Books a payment; an empty one is dropped, and its offset still commits with the window. struct Book; impl Handle<Payment, LedgerEntry> for Book { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<LedgerEntry, HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.cents == 0 { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(LedgerEntry { payment_id: payment.id, cents: payment.cents, })) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_eos_replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("ledger-svc"), |b| { // The transform carries each delivery's coordinates onto its reply, where the pipeline // pairs them. b.include(book) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("ledger-1")) .transform(EosReplies) }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_eos_replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("ledger-svc"), |b| { let payments = subscriber("payments", Book) .map_source(|_| { KafkaTopic::new("payments").commit(Commit::Transactional("ledger-1".into())) }) .reply() .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); // The transform carries each delivery's coordinates onto its reply, where the pipeline // pairs them. b.include(payments.build()) .out_reply(EosPublish::new("ledger-1")) .transform(EosReplies) }, ) }

per_partition gives each source partition its own transactional publisher, so a worker pool runs independent transactions. It turns the policy into a KafkaPartitionedPublish, named PartitionedPublish in the prelude. The transactional id becomes a base: the publisher of partition 3 is fenced by "{base}-p3". A handler bounds its slot Out<impl PartitionLanes> and reads its delivery's partition through Ctx<Partition>. PartitionLanes::for_partition returns that partition's publisher, created and initialized on first use. The live value is TransactionalPartitions, and its clones share the publishers. The scope is the source partition because one producer runs one transaction at a time. Under the default LaneKey::Partition, a workers(n, by_key) pool processes each partition in order on one lane, so each lane has a transaction of its own. The set of ids follows the topic's partitions, not the worker count: changing n keeps the ids and their fencing. It does not combine with LaneKey::RecordKey, which spreads one partition over several lanes; two lanes would then meet on one producer and get KafkaError::TransactionBusy. What a lane publishes leaves through the partition's own publisher, so a test reads it on the topic, not on the slot's record.

An invoice's lines are published in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs /// Bills every line of an invoice in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. #[subscriber( KafkaTopic::new("invoice-batches").commit(Commit::Tracked), workers(4, by_key) )] async fn bill( invoice: &Invoice, Ctx(partition): Ctx<Partition>, Out(lanes): Out<impl PartitionLanes>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(lane) = lanes.for_partition(partition).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; if lane.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } for &amount in &invoice.amounts { let entry = InvoiceLine { invoice_id: invoice.id, amount, }; if lane.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { lane.abort().await.ok(); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } if lane.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs /// Bills every line of an invoice in the transaction of the invoice's source partition. struct Bill; impl<L> Handle<Invoice, (), Outs<(L,)>, KafkaContext> for Bill where L: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: PartitionLanes>, { async fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, ctx: &mut Context<'_, KafkaContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let partition = ctx.context(Partition); let Ok(lane) = outs.get(DefaultSlot).for_partition(partition).await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; if lane.begin_transaction().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } for &amount in &invoice.amounts { let entry = InvoiceLine { invoice_id: invoice.id, amount, }; if lane.message(&entry).publish().await.is_err() { lane.abort().await.ok(); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } if lane.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs fn app(servers: &str) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group("billing-svc"), |b| { // One transactional id per source partition: "billing-svc-1-p0", "billing-svc-1-p1". let lanes = Publish::default() .transactional_id("billing-svc-1") .per_partition(); b.include(bill).out(DefaultSlot, lanes).build() }, ) } examples/manual/kafka_transactions_partitions.rs fn app(servers: &str) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( KafkaBroker::new([servers]).default_group("billing-svc"), |b| { // One transactional id per source partition: "billing-svc-1-p0", "billing-svc-1-p1". let lanes = Publish::default() .transactional_id("billing-svc-1") .per_partition(); let invoices = subscriber("invoice-batches", Bill) .map_source(|_| KafkaTopic::new("invoice-batches").commit(Commit::Tracked)) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); b.include(invoices.build()).out(DefaultSlot, lanes).build() }, ) }

Это руководство выбирает, что фиксируют ack и nack в Kafka: собственную фиксацию librdkafka, точное at-least-once с Commit::Tracked или пакеты, которые завершаются поэлементно. Kafka не завершает отдельные сообщения. Группа консьюмеров фиксирует позицию в каждой партиции, и всё, что ниже неё, считается прочитанным. Обработчик всё равно завершает каждую доставку, поэтому режим Commit подписки решает, как эти завершения превращаются в позицию. Режим ack drop retry После падения Auto (по умолчанию) ничего ничего сообщает, что не поддерживается, и запись не возвращается хвост обработанных записей читается заново, или сохранённые, но не обработанные записи пропускаются Tracked завершает смещение завершает смещение запись возвращается каждая незавершённая запись читается заново Transactional завершает смещение, которое фиксируется с транзакцией конвейера то же, что ack задерживает окно до срока транзакции открытое окно читается заново Пример - сервис выплат: выплаты терять нельзя, а просмотры страниц можно. Третий режим описан в руководстве Транзакции и exactly-once.

pay_out отправляет выплату через банк и отвечает подтверждением. Если банк не ответил, выплата возвращается и обрабатывается снова. Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payouts.done")] struct Paid { payout_id: u64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("payouts").commit(Commit::Tracked), reply)] async fn pay_out(payout: &Payout, State(bank): State<Arc<Bank>>) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { if payout.amount_cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if bank.0.call().await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payout.id, "bank unavailable, payout comes back"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout sent"); Ok(Paid { payout_id: payout.id, }) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payout { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Paid { payout_id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Paid { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payouts.done"; } impl MessageHeaders for Paid { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Paid { const NAME: &'static str = "Paid"; } struct PayOut; impl Handle<Payout, Paid, (), (), Clients> for PayOut { async fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<Paid, HandlerOutcome> { if payout.amount_cents == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if ctx.state().bank.call().await.is_err() { tracing::warn!(payout.id, "bank unavailable, payout comes back"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(payout.id, payout.amount_cents, "payout sent"); Ok(Paid { payout_id: payout.id, }) } } При Commit::Tracked ack поднимает зафиксированную позицию до самой ранней доставки, которая ещё не завершена. Подтверждения от параллельных воркеров приходят в любом порядке, а позиция никогда не обгоняет выплату, которая ещё выполняется. retry возвращает доставку подписке, и та доставляет её снова раньше всего, что выберет дальше. До тех пор её смещение остаётся незавершённым, поэтому позиция за него не уходит. Если процесс остановится раньше, после нового запуска Kafka вернёт ему эту выплату. Поэтому выплата никогда не теряется, но может быть обработана дважды: до падения и после него. Вызов банка должен принимать повторную выплату, например распознавая её по идентификатору. retry без предела попыток возвращает запись бесконечно. Предел добавляет руководство Повторы и темы dead-letter.

count_view считает просмотры страниц в хранилище аналитики. Потерянный просмотр здесь не важен, поэтому подписка остаётся в режиме по умолчанию. Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct PageView { page: String, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("page-views").group("analytics"))] async fn count_view(view: &PageView, State(counters): State<Arc<Counters>>) -> HandlerOutcome { if counters.0.call().await.is_err() { // Under `Commit::Auto` nothing brings the view back; analytics accepts the loss. return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::debug!(page = %view.page, "page view counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct PageView { page: String, } struct CountView; impl Handle<PageView, (), (), (), Clients> for CountView { async fn handle( &self, view: &PageView, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if ctx.state().counters.call().await.is_err() { // Under `Commit::Auto` nothing brings the view back; analytics accepts the loss. return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::debug!(page = %view.page, "page view counted"); Ok(()) } } При Commit::Auto librdkafka сохраняет позицию, когда отдаёт запись приложению, и фиксирует её по таймеру. ack и drop ничего не меняют. retry сообщает, что не поддерживается, и просмотр не возвращается. Этот режим самый дешёвый. Зато при падении можно потерять обработанные записи или пропустить записи, которые были сохранены, но не обработаны.

reconcile принимает строки выписки пакетами до 500 штук и завершает каждую строку отдельно. Макросы Вручную src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct StatementLine { payout_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(KafkaTopic::new("statements").group("reconciliation").commit(Commit::Tracked))] async fn reconcile(lines: &[StatementLine]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { lines .iter() .map(|line| { if line.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(line.payout_id, "empty statement line dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() }) .collect() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct StatementLine { payout_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[StatementLine], (), (), (), Clients> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, lines: &[StatementLine], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { if lines.iter().all(|line| line.amount_cents > 0) { return ready(Ok(())); } let outcomes = lines .iter() .map(|line| { if line.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(line.payout_id, "empty statement line dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() }) .collect(); ready(Err(outcomes)) } } Пакет - это одна доставка и записи, которые librdkafka уже выбрала, без дополнительного ожидания. Поэтому он часто меньше размера, заданного в точке монтирования. Возвращённый список завершает пакет поэлементно. В ручной форме Ok(()) подтверждает все элементы, а Err(outcomes) завершает каждый по-своему. При Commit::Tracked элемент, который просит повтор, возвращается один, и зафиксированная позиция стоит перед ним, пока он не завершится. Если процесс остановится раньше, подтверждённые элементы после него будут прочитаны снова: это дубликаты, а не потери. Сколько записей librdkafka держит в очереди, определяет свойство консьюмера, которое задаёт KafkaTopic::config. Когда очередь полна, librdkafka приостанавливает выборку на fetch.queue.backoff.ms (по умолчанию 1000 мс), и большие записи за медленным обработчиком замедляются. .config("fetch.queue.backoff.ms", "10") сокращает эту паузу.
